title: Describing someone
topic: physical description and character; être, avoir, porter
why: After the family, you learn to describe the people around you: their height, hair and eyes, what they wear, and their personality. The lesson reviews adjective agreement with new irregular feminines and shows why French says « il a les yeux bleus » where English says “he has blue eyes”.

{"lessons": ["

What does he look like?

To ask what someone is like, French has one very common question: Il est comment ? / Elle est comment ? It covers both looks and personality, like English “What's he like?” and “What does he look like?” at the same time. The answer starts with être + adjective, and the adjective agrees with the person, as you know.

MasculineFeminineEnglish
grandgrandetall
petitpetiteshort, small
minceminceslim
jeunejeuneyoung
brunbrunedark-haired
blondblondeblond, fair-haired
rouxroussered-haired

Listen to the feminine: the final consonant, silent in the masculine, is heard when an e follows: grand / grande, petit / petite, blond / blonde. Mince and jeune already end in e, so they don't change. Roux has an irregular feminine: rousse.

Mon frère est grand et brun. Ma sœur est petite et blonde.My brother is tall and dark-haired. My sister is short and blond.

False friend: brun describes hair, not skin or eyes. Il est brun = he has dark (brown or black) hair. For brown eyes, you'll use another word, marron, on the next screen.

", "

Eyes, hair, glasses: avoir and porter

For eyes and hair, English says “he has blue eyes”. French also uses avoir, but with the definite article les, not des and not a possessive: Il a les yeux bleus. Learn this pattern as a block.

FrenchEnglish
Il a les yeux bleus / verts / noirs.He has blue / green / black eyes.
Elle a les yeux marron.She has brown eyes.
Elle a les cheveux longs / courts.She has long / short hair.
Il a les cheveux frisés.He has curly hair.
Elle a les cheveux blonds / bruns / roux / gris.She has blond / dark / red / gray hair.

Three details: les yeux is the plural of un œil (one eye); les cheveux is masculine plural, so its adjectives take -s (courts, longs, frisés); and marron never changes: les yeux marron. You can combine two adjectives with et: Elle a les cheveux longs et frisés.

Porter: glasses, a beard, clothes

Porter (a regular -er verb) means to wear: Il porte des lunettes (He wears glasses), Il porte une barbe, Elle porte une robe rouge. You can also say Il a une barbe.

Ressembler à: to look like

“I look like my mother” is Je ressemble à ma mère: no “look”, and a compulsory à, which contracts as usual: Tu ressembles au voisin, Ils ressemblent à leurs parents.

Léa ressemble à son père : elle a les yeux verts et les cheveux roux.Léa looks like her father: she has green eyes and red hair.
", "

Personality

Many character adjectives have a feminine that is more than just an added e. These endings come back in hundreds of adjectives, so they're worth learning now.

EndingMasculineFeminineEnglish
-eux → -eusesérieuxsérieuseserious
-il → -illegentilgentillekind, nice
-if → -ivesportifsportivesporty, athletic
-eur → -eusetravailleurtravailleusehardworking
-et → -ètediscretdiscrètediscreet, reserved
-e (no change)drôledrôlefunny
-e (no change)timidetimideshy

Gentil is pronounced with a silent l (“zhan-tee”), but gentille ends with a y sound (“zhan-tee-y”). Sérieux doesn't change in the masculine plural: mes frères sont sérieux.

In everyday speech, you'll hear sympa all the time: it's short for sympathique and has the same form for a man and a woman: Il est sympa, Elle est sympa. Careful: sympathique means nice, friendly, not “sympathetic”.

Putting it all together

Remember the position of adjectives: these all go after the noun (une fille sportive, un garçon timide), while the short group grand, petit, jeune, beau goes before: une jeune femme sérieuse, un grand garçon sportif.

Ma cousine est grande et mince. Elle a les cheveux courts et elle porte des lunettes. Elle est très gentille, mais un peu timide.My cousin is tall and slim. She has short hair and wears glasses. She's very kind, but a little shy.

To soften a description, French people love un peu (a little) and assez (quite): Il est un peu timide, Elle est assez grande.
